To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

low CCH concentrations induce oscillating Vm in pancreatic acinar (rat) cells, that Vm oscillations follow the Nernst potentials for Cl– (Ecl-) and for nonselective cations (ENaCl), and that whole cell conductance is maximal when Vm oscillates towards ECl– and minimal when Vm approaches ENaCl.

(1) CCH induces oscillations of membrane potential towards ECl– in the absence of Na+, and (2) CCH-induced oscillations of membrane conductance are maximal when the membrane is depolarized towards ECl–.

(i) the Vm of pancreatic acinar cells depolarizes in oscillating fashion towards Ecl– but not the Nernst for nonselective cations when low concentrations of acetylcholine are used, and (ii) this suggests that NaCl secretion is not mediated by the ‘push-poll’ model in these cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanism of fluid secretion by pancreatic acinar cells.
the mechanisms of fluid secretion in pancreatic exocrine cells.
the mechanisms of NaCl transport in the exocrine pancreas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ‘push’ mechanism (i.e. Cl– extrusion) is probably not the primary driving force for CCH-induced fluid secretion in pancreatic acini.

CCH-induced Na+ and Cl- secretion in the pancreas is probably mediated by the activation of Cl- channels in the luminal membrane and Na+ channels and nonselective cations channels in the basolateral membranes.

the ‘push’ phase of the ‘push-poll’ model for acetylcholine-stimulated Cl– secretion in rat pancreatic acini is probably mediated by a nonselective conductance, whereas the ‘pull’ phase may be mediated by the basolateral Cl– conductance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ‘push’ phase is likely to be due to Cl- secretion via a cAMP-dependent Cl- conductance, and the ‘pull’ phase to a cAMP-dependent nonselective catio channel.

in pancreatic acinar cell NaCl secretion is induced by acetylcholine (ACh) via two mechanisms, one involving the activation of a Ca2+-dependent Cl channel (CaCC) and a second one involving the activation or recruitment of an unknown Cl- channel.
CCH induces oscillating depolarization to ECl– in rat pancreatic acini, but not to ECl– + ENa+.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Vm oscillations are due to a change in conductance, which can be explained by the opening and closing of a nonselective ion channel, rather than a change in ion concentrations.
the ‘push’ and the ‘pull’ phases of the ‘push-pulls’ concept are not necessarily separated temporally and spatially in the same cell.
CCH induces oscillations of Vm towards ECl-, but not the predicted Nernste potential for a non-selective cation channel.
